newsitem.title: CROATIA: Refugee threat to force way back to Croat enclave.
newsitem.headline: Refugee threat to force way back to Croat enclave.

text.p: Croat refugees threatened on Tuesday to force their way back into Croatia's last Serb-held enclave unless U.N. peace troops leave by January and local elections are held by mid-December.

A U.N. administration backed by 5,000 peace troops moved into the Eastern Slavonia region last January with the task of gradually reinstating Croatian government rule there in one year, with the option of up to a year's extension if needed.
Croatia's nationalist government said recently it would accept, if reluctantly, a three-month extension to April 15, 1997 recommended by the U.N. administrator of the region.
The U.N. Security Council will decide the issue next month.

Zagreb has also agreed to holding elections early in the new year after earlier insisting on a December 15 deadline. U.N. officials said last week it would be all but impossible to organise a free and fair vote in the next two months.

In that context, the demand by the association of Croat war refugees to forcibly return to their homes seemed mainly a symbolic manoeuvre, orchestrated or encouraged by nationalist hardliners in the government, to underline to U.N. policymakers the urgency of the situation.

The right-wing association represents 80,000 Croats driven out of Eastern Slavonia when it was captured by minority Serbs in a 1991 rebellion against Croatia's declaration of independence from federal Yugoslavia.
HINA, the Croatian state news agency, said the Croatian Association of Displaced People (ZPH) issued a statement setting out the conclusions of a conference on Saturday.

"The ZPH demanded that the elections for local self-government bodies in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srijem be held by 15 December 1996, in line with the 1991 census and existing Croatian laws," the statement said.

"Unless the U.N. Security Council adopts a resolution verifying the agreements between Croatia and the international community on the expiry of the mandate of the U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), displaced people will organise the return by themselves after 15 January 1997."
Any forced return of Croats to the fertile plain on Croatia's Danube River border with rump Yugoslavia would almost certainly trigger violence with local Serbs.

The Croatian minister in charge of Eastern Slavonia's reintegration said after last week's talks with UNTAES administrator Jacques Klein, a U.S. diplomat, that Zagreb envisaged resettling all refugees peacefully during 1997.

In its first nine months, UNTAES has disarmed Serb separatist militia, created a joint Serb-Croat police force under its supervision, restored telecommunications and postal links across old ceasefire lines and helped Croat officials set up social welfare and citizenship offices in the enclave.
Of Eastern Slavonia's 190,000 residents in 1991, Croats formed the largest community followed closely by Serbs.

At least one quarter of the estimated 120,000 Serbs now in Eastern Slavonia are refugees from other rebel pockets of Croatia retaken in government offensives in 1995, and Zagreb has said they must leave to allow Croat refugees to return home.
